I’ve made ten jars like this, crimson pots, thrown crimson clay that’ll eventually be coated in a crimson glaze and then finally, they’ll be reduction fired, oh, there’s also some bronze in the mix, small fragments, which when put through the kiln turn into these red haloed flecks of metal. All of that might sound quite over the top but it’s a deep red with underlying tones of black and hopefully they resemble some of the tests I’ve fired in the past… fingers crossed. They require a different approach when crafting them, especially during the turning stage. As the particles of grog the body contains are constantly torn out I have to go back over the surface, burnishing it and smoothing it as I go to get rid of the overly prominent scratches these splinters of ceramic create. I lost a few pieces from attempting to fix oval openings, they were thrown round, but as clay slowly dries it’s quite common for it to subtlety warp. I tried to gentle press the opening back into a round shape and I felt something give; upon further inspection I found a hairline crack in the rim. Grogged clays might be tough during the throwing and the firing but it’s brittle stuff during the trimming stage, especially when trimmed as thinly as this. #clay #handmade #satisfying #pottery #ceramics

pricing my work is truly my LEAST favourite thing 😭  especially after trying to look closer at the numbers behind my small ceramic business. i’m trying to map out the potential 1, 3, and 5 year revenue and expense projections to see if investing in a kiln and building this business actually makes any sense. at my current $30-$65 price point, i’m losing money selling my work and cannot justify a kiln. i’ve made the terrifying decision to raise my prices by 25-30%. the money will go towards expanding production (investing. in a kiln & shelving), upgrading my website, expanding to ship to the US, and finally, offering private lessons and workshops.  with the price increase, I will still need to survive 6 months - 1 year without a livable wage / making profit. i’ll be focusing on my higher-margin petal bowls and bring in some more affordable $25 products like spoon rests and trinket dishes to keep things as accessible as possible. my mugs are not viable as they take me 2hrs each, but i’m going to keep making them for now and hope i can speed it up. no more lidded jars outside of speciality collections as the margins are too low.  i’m also going to try to secure 1-2 freelance social media clients to provide me with some supplement income as a buffer. this is the behind the scenes of small ceramics business’ that you normally don’t see, because it’s not nearly as cute or fun as the pots themselves. #potterybusiness #ceramics #smallbusiness #priceincrease #handmadeceramics

A simple way to add a lock to a regular flat lid. This locking system is made entirely from clay and keeps the lid in place without changing the look of the piece. I love simple solutions like this - especially when they disappear into the design. I prefer to fire the lid upside down, standing on the knob. This allows me to apply a thin layer of glaze to the bottom of the lid, the locking tabs, and the gallery, creating a smoother, more cohesive look when the piece is open. #pottery #ceramics

Did you know that you are not limited just by the size of your kiln when making large ceramics! The best way to build big pottery in my opinion his with coils. I’m making a floor lamp for a client and decided that stacking multiple pieces was how I was going to get the hight required for a piece of clay furniture! In my YouTube video this weekend I’m recreating some pots I haven’t thrown since 2014, specially store jars with inset, internal galleries and thin lids with thrown knobs. You can find a link to the fully narrated video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   I’ve lied a little bit. I did create jars that were similar to this during my apprenticeship with Lisa Hammond between 2014-2017, yet they were bellied pieces with a gallery closer to the jars I make these days, yet they unusual thrown knobs that were in themselves similar to small bowls.   To create pots with internal galleries like this you need to split the rim. One section becomes the lip, the other is coaxed inside and carefully set horizontal to essentially become a ledge onto which the lid can be held aloft. This alone is a tricky task and it involves throwing a form with enough material in the lip to withstand such a manoeuvre. Secondly, there’s the small disc-like lid, a form that’s thrown off-the-hump and then the following day it’s trimmed back to have its more exacting shape and the knob is thrown on, again, a tricky task as it involves fiddly, fingertip throwing and a lot of accuracy.   All of this and more will be covered in my longer, narrated YouTube upload. I enjoyed making these and since it has been such a long time since I’ve crafted them, my skillset in the interim has improved massively, thus I could apply newly learnt techniques and ability into making shapes I used to struggle with to some degree. I hope you like the film if you happen to click over and watch it, it’s greatly appreciated if you do as it helps to keep the lights on in the workshop.   #pottery #ceramics #handmade #jar #satisfying

I could write a book about making teapots, and I still don’t consider mine to be very good. Every time I make a batch, I can see things to improve upon, I suppose the issue is not making them nearly often enough, in a way, if I spent a month making nothing but teapots, I imagine they’d improve tremendously, but who has time for that?   These are some tips on the subject of teapot making, there’s also a number of videos on my YouTube channel that discuss their craft in obscene detail, (a few of those films are almost an hour long).   The teapot in question in this video is a very simple one, twice fired, hence the intense green colour the vessel has, because of an area of patchy glaze the pot initially had. The second reduction fired fixed it, mostly, the glaze melts and moves again, and the iron bearing clay underneath intensifies, as do the droplets on the surface, making for a slightly more metallic finish overall. It glitters and gleams a bit more and it turns iridescent where the feldspathic glaze breaks on the sharp clay-work underneath.   All in all, a good teapot, but I’ve kept a few notes on what to change when I next throw a batch.   #teapot #teaware #celadon #pottery #handmade #ceramics

Here’s a completed apothecary jar and a full overview of how it’s made. For this type of lidded jar, the base and lid are thrown from one continuous piece of clay, then cut open and trimmed to create the inner edges and gallery so the lid doesn’t slide off. I like this type of piece because it has a continuous line from the base to the top of the knob. If you’d like to see a far more thorough exploration of these vases, I recommend watching the 40-minute version that’s on my YouTube channel, a link to which you can find via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   This week I’m making some of my favourite pots, they aren’t really about function, at least that is not what I’m thinking about whilst I create them. These angular vases with a protruding line across one side are simple, decorative objects and a welcome change after a few weeks of focusing solely on functional ware. I take my time with them and pay close attention to proportion and surface and how the line travels and over the past few years they’ve changed quite a lot.   They used to appear squatter and the lines were heavier and less defined but after making many batches, they have gradually become taller and more refined, in my opinion. The carved line has followed that shift, it’s sharper now, more deliberate and despite only being a relatively small addition, the change it makes is drastic. Most of my work is thrown on the wheel and naturally symmetrical and therefore this detail interrupts that uniformity. It gives the vessel a direction and a front. It catches the light and throws a shadow across the flat planes and somehow that single line makes the pots feel more figurative, especially when they are grouped together.   If you happen to click over and watch the longer edition, thank you, it means so much!   #pottery #vase #sculpture #handmade #ceramics

Colanders, strainers, even berry bowls are quite popular. I make a few types of small medium and large colanders, but have really enjoyed making these strainer bowls. The shape is more of a basket or bassinet in which the strainer holes are only at the upper half of the bowl. This allows the fruit or veggies to be fully submerged in water before tipping and pouring out without spilling the produce. #pottery #studioceramics #wheelthrown #berrybowl #potteryartist
